subject: chemistry

moments.title: Payen and Persoz isolate diastase
moments.who: Anselme Payen and Jean-François Persoz, Paris
moments.body:
They extract a substance from malt that converts starch into sugar. They call it diastase ('separation' in Greek). It's the first isolated enzyme — though they don't know what they have.

For decades enzymes are treated as mysterious 'ferments' — substances that act without being consumed, but whose nature is unclear.
moments.takeaway: Cells contain catalysts. We don't yet understand what they are.

moments.title: Emil Fischer's lock and key
moments.body:
Fischer is studying sugar chemistry. He finds different enzymes act on different sugar stereoisomers — emulsin cleaves alpha-glycosides; invertase cleaves beta-glycosides. He proposes enzymes have a specific shape that fits their substrates.

Fischer's analogy: lock and key. Only the right key fits.

quote.text: To use a picture I will say that enzyme and glucoside must fit into each other like a lock and key.

moments.takeaway: Catalytic specificity comes from molecular shape. The seeds of structural biology.

moments.title: Sumner crystallises urease
moments.body:
Until 1926, leading biochemists (notably Richard Willstätter) insist enzymes are not proteins — proteins are too 'simple' to have catalytic activity.

Sumner crystallises urease from jack beans and shows it's a pure protein, fully catalytically active. The biochemical community largely ignores him. By the mid-1930s, more enzymes have been crystallised and shown to be proteins, and Sumner's work is accepted. He gets the 1946 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: Enzymes are proteins. Even Nobel-Prize-winning insights have to fight resistance.

moments.title: Koshland's induced fit
moments.body: Fischer's lock-and-key model can't explain why some 'small' molecules fit certain enzymes that 'should' have room for them but don't react. Koshland proposes the enzyme CHANGES SHAPE when it binds the right substrate — induced fit. Wrong substrates don't trigger the conformational change and don't react.
moments.takeaway: Enzymes are dynamic. They don't just hold substrates — they reorganise around them.

moments.title: First protein structure — lysozyme
moments.who: David Phillips and team, Royal Institution, London
moments.body:
Phillips and colleagues solve the X-ray crystal structure of hen egg-white lysozyme at 2.0 angstrom resolution. It's the first enzyme structure ever determined.

They can see the active site, model substrate binding and propose a mechanism — making physical sense of decades of kinetic data.
moments.takeaway: We can now see enzymes at atomic resolution. Biochemistry becomes structural biology.

now.title: Enzymes today
now.body:
Over 7,000 enzymes are catalogued. Their structures (more than 200,000 in the Protein Data Bank) are routinely solved by X-ray crystallography or cryo-electron microscopy. AlphaFold (DeepMind, 2020) predicts protein structures with near-experimental accuracy.

We engineer enzymes for industrial use (laundry detergent proteases, cellulose breakdown for biofuels, drug synthesis). Frances Arnold won the 2018 Nobel Prize for directed evolution — letting selection design enzymes for us.
now.open_questions: Can we design enzymes from scratch (de novo) for any reaction we want? How do enzymes achieve rate accelerations of 10 to the 17 or more compared to uncatalysed reactions? Why are so many enzyme structures conserved across billion-year evolutionary timescales?

reflection: Sumner's discovery that enzymes are proteins was rejected by the leading biochemist of the day (Willstätter, a Nobel laureate). For 8 years the community sided with the famous man over the right one. How does science recover from situations where authority overrides evidence?
